about: Authored choices and notes for the periodic table. scripts/build-chem-data.mjs reads this file and fails on anything in it that it does not recognise. isotopeMasses: for each element with no CIAAW standard atomic weight, the isotope whose mass PubChem prints, and whether that mass is an estimate. covalentRadius: for each element whose covalent radius the source lists more than once, the value shown, which must be the first listed. notes: sentences shown on the element card, each beside the row it qualifies (a field name of the element record) and each with the id of the source that supports it. A note must sit on a value the element has; a note marked valueAbsent is about a value the source leaves empty, and must sit on an empty one.

notes.text: Helium becomes solid only under pressure. At ordinary pressure it stays liquid however far it is cooled.
At ordinary pressure carbon does not melt: it turns from solid straight to gas. PubChem's carbon page labels this figure as diamond's.
At ordinary pressure carbon turns from solid straight to gas, so this is not the boiling point of a liquid. PubChem's carbon page also lists 3800 °C, which is 4073 K, marked as sublimation.
This is the density of graphite. Diamond is denser: the CRC Handbook and Lange's Handbook give 3.513 g/cm³ for it, as transcribed on Wikipedia's data page.
PubChem's phosphorus page labels this figure as white phosphorus's.
PubChem's phosphorus page labels this figure as white phosphorus's.
This is the density of white phosphorus: the CRC Handbook and Lange's Handbook give 1.823 g/cm³ for it, and higher figures for red and black phosphorus, as transcribed on Wikipedia's data page.

Measured under pressure: liquid arsenic forms only above atmospheric pressure. At ordinary pressure arsenic turns from solid straight to gas at 887 K, which is why this is higher than its boiling point.
At ordinary pressure arsenic turns from solid straight to gas at this temperature. It does not boil from a liquid.

PubChem's flerovium page also lists a boiling point of about 210 K. That is below room temperature, so by that figure flerovium would be a gas, not a solid.
PubChem's oganesson page also lists a boiling point of 350 ± 30 K, marked as extrapolated. That is above room temperature, so by that figure oganesson would not be a gas.

PubChem's copernicium page also lists a boiling point of about 357 K, with an uncertainty of about 110 K either way. That range reaches below room temperature, so by that figure copernicium could be a gas.
Only compounds of aluminum, such as alum, were known in ancient times. PubChem's aluminum page says the metal was first isolated, in impure form, in 1825.
Only compounds of calcium, such as lime, were known in ancient times. PubChem's calcium page says the metal was first isolated in 1808.
PubChem's fluorine page says that a fluorine compound was first recorded in use about 1670, and that the element was first isolated in 1886.
1854 is when crystalline silicon was first prepared. PubChem's silicon page says amorphous silicon was discovered in 1824.

PubChem puts the last electron in 6d. NIST lists a different ground state, [Rn]5f14 7s2 7p1, with that electron in 7p.

PubChem's table puts astatine with the halogens, its group. PubChem's own astatine page classes it as a semi-metal; the lighter halogens are nonmetals.
